Hello, thanks for taking the time to talk with me today. To get started, which company do you work for, and could you walk me through what an ordinary working day looks like for you from start to finish?
transcript.answer: I work at one of the drone operating companies that uses the platform's shared service. As a dispatcher, my day involves planning and running flights, including deciding which drone flies and along which way, and signing off a flight before it leaves. Several of us often plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight if needed.

transcript.question: Could you walk me through a concrete example of one flight from the moment you find out it needs to happen until it finishes—who hands the work to you, and who do you hand things off to along the way?
Let's break that down: how do you know what flights you need to plan when you start your shift, and how do you interact with the fleet technicians or the airspace desk?
Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day at work, and what made it so bad?
transcript.answer: I worry when the authorities announce a sudden airspace closure or amend an existing one while my drones are already in the air. Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on.

transcript.question: Could you tell me about a specific day recently when several of those things happened at once—what actually occurred and how did you handle it?
When you are signing off a flight or monitoring it, what do you currently check by hand because you don't trust the systems or data you have?

When you mentioned that several of you often plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, how do you make sure you don't double-book a drone or a site, or run into other problems before signing off a flight?
When something does go wrong with a flight or a drone, what is the very first information you need to know right after it happens?
Thinking about a new service being built for your work, what are you most afraid it might do wrong or make harder for you?
transcript.answer: I worry that software might be built to choose a drone or a way for us to fly, which goes against our company policy that software never does that. I also worry about the service running on a single server that is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and that occasionally crashes.

transcript.question: Why does your company have the policy that software must never choose the drone or the route, and what do you look at when you make those choices yourself?
transcript.answer: Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility as a dispatcher. Our company policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us.

transcript.question: When you sign off a flight before it leaves, what needs to be true before you are allowed to sign it off?
When you call off a flight, what are the reasons you do that, and what happens to a drone if it is already in the air when you call it off?
transcript.answer: I can call off a flight, but I don't know the reasons why I do that or what happens to a drone if it is already in the air when I call it off.

transcript.question: You mentioned earlier that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all, and that drones sometimes restart in flight. How does that affect you while you are running flights?
You also mentioned that the platform is shared by several competing companies. What are your concerns or rules around what other companies can see about your flights, drones, or sites?
transcript.answer: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. We accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

transcript.question: Is there anything else about your work as a dispatcher, the flights, the drones, or the airspace that we haven't covered yet?
transcript.answer: I worry that a closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. I also worry that radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all.

transcript.question: Could you walk me through what an ordinary working day looks like for you, from start to finish?
When you first sit down at the airspace desk for your shift, what is the very first thing you do?
How would you describe your role at the airspace desk?
transcript.answer: I keep the shared picture of the airspace. This includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations.

transcript.question: How do you get the information about closures from the authorities?
When a closure is announced by the authorities, what do you do with that information?
transcript.answer: I enter closures announced by the authorities into our shared picture of the airspace. When I enter a closure, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

transcript.question: What kind of details tell you how much disruption a closure caused, without you looking into any one company's operations?
Besides entering closures, what do you do with the flight corridors and the zones that group them?
transcript.answer: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which is the network of flight corridors between sites and the zones that group them.

transcript.question: When do you need to add or change a flight corridor or a zone?
Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day on the job, and what made it so bad?
What kinds of things can go wrong in your work at the airspace desk?
Right after something goes wrong in the airspace or with a closure, what is the first thing you need to know?
What do you currently check by hand because you do not trust the existing tools or information?
When we build this new service, what are you most afraid it might get wrong?

What information defines a flight corridor or a zone in the shared picture?
Is there anything else about your work at the airspace desk or what you need from the service that you can tell me?
transcript.answer: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, including the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

items.requirement: The service must isolate each operating company's data so that a company's fleet, jobs, sites, charging pads, and operational problems are visible and accessible only to that company and never exposed to competing companies.
The service must prevent airspace desk personnel from viewing or accessing any individual operating company's private operations, fleet, jobs, sites, or problems.

The service must allow fleet technicians to register new drones into their company's fleet (supporting fleets of several hundred drones per company) and record each drone's manufacturer, model, payload capacity, flight range on a full battery, installed sensors, charging connector type, and home site.
The service must allow fleet technicians to retire old drones from their company's fleet so that retired drones can no longer be assigned to flights or operations.
The service must allow fleet technicians to take a drone out of service for repairs and servicing, and to return the drone to active service when repairs are complete.

The service must allow fleet technicians to register and set up charging pads at their company's sites (supporting several dozen charging pads per company), including specifying the charging connector type for each pad.

The service must allow fleet technicians to assign a drone to a charging pad to charge only if the charging pad belongs to the same company and has the exact same charging connector type as the drone, because connector types are not interchangeable and companies never lend pads to other companies.

The service must allow dispatchers to plan flights by manually selecting the specific drone and the flight path (corridors) for the flight, and the service must never automatically select or assign a drone or a flight path on behalf of a dispatcher.
The service must allow a dispatcher to sign off a planned flight before it departs, and allow a dispatcher to call off a flight when needed.

The service must handle concurrent flight planning by multiple dispatchers within the same company so that popular drones and busy sites or resources cannot be conflictingly double-booked when flights are planned and signed off.

The service must process incoming drone telemetry and flight reports in a way that tolerates patchy radio coverage and mid-flight drone software restarts—specifically handling reports that arrive late, arrive out of chronological order, arrive multiple times (duplicates), or are missing—without corrupting the tracked state of the flight or drone.
The service must track actual reported battery levels during flight rather than relying solely on planned battery consumption, accounting for faster battery drain caused by cold or wind.

The service must allow the airspace desk to maintain a shared airspace picture visible to all customer companies, consisting of the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group those corridors, and airspace closures announced by the authorities.

The service must allow the airspace desk to enter new airspace closures and amend existing closures announced by the authorities, including closures that take effect immediately while drones from one or more companies are already in the air.

When an airspace closure is entered or amended, the service must immediately identify affected planned and in-flight operations so that dispatchers are alerted when their active or planned flights are impacted by the closure.

When the airspace desk enters or amends an airspace closure, the service must provide the airspace desk with an aggregated measure of how much disruption the closure caused across all customer companies without revealing any individual company's identity or private operational details.

The service must persist flight, fleet, and airspace state durably so that server updates, restarts during working hours, or unexpected server crashes do not lose or corrupt the state of active flights in the air, planned flights, fleet records, or airspace closures.
